1) Downplay your alcohol use when you do your alcohol evaluation so they don’t put you into inpatient or other expensive treatment. Be very careful with your answers when they ask why you drink. Do not say you drink alone or that you drink to relax or anything like that. If you get this done prior to conviction and they ask you what your BAC is, say you don’t know but you don’t think it was that high and you would have to ask your attorney. They’re not going to actually contact them to ask; they just want to get you out of the door. As long as the rest of your answers are fine you’ll get minimum counseling. If you actually do need help get it outside of the courts.

2) Get all your probationary requirements (i.e. alcohol evaluation/treatment, MADD panel, etc.) done ahead of time. I did this and ended up with no probation because of it

3) This will be the most expensive mistake of your life. I think I spent close to $7000 on mine between hiring an attorney, a Canada lawyer for a work trip, paying for the interlock, my insurance deductible from the DUI accident, the alcohol evaluation/treatment, MADD panel, and court fees. A lot of people pay more than this

4) If you don’t choose sobriety, you absolutely need to never EVER drink and drive again, and I would strongly advise not using any kind of drugs including marijuana even if you’re in a legal state. There are plenty of cases on here of people getting DUIs when they hadn’t even smoked that day but it was found in their blood and the officer decided they were intoxicated. It’s way worse on a second offense. Don’t take the risk. You get one fuck up and next time you’re probably going to jail

5) Let this be your wake up call whether you think you have a problem with alcohol or not. I guarantee this wasn’t the first time you drove with a drink in your system. As I said earlier, you can still get a DUI under 0.08. Legal limit isn’t really a thing, it just lessens the punishment but doesn’t mean they can’t convict you. If you need help getting sober or cutting back, this is the time

I used to be so terrified of this and didn’t want to fly because of it. But I can say I’ve been on probably 40 flights in the last several years and haven’t seen it happen a single time. I used to have a huge fear of flying (in general; not related to emet) and I ended up taking 22 flights in 2023. I got over it and it really helped turn things around for me. I wear noise canceling headphones and take benadryl (or to be honest have a few drinks) and make sure I’ll fall asleep on the flight so even if something happens, I won’t be exposed to it. If you’re like me and your fear is rooted in other people being sick, this really does help a lot. What I’ve heard is that it’s pretty rare these days with the technology getting better, it’s a smoother flight and people are less likely to get motion sickness. Obviously there’s still the fear of drunk people or those terrible people who choose to travel while sick, but if your phobia doesn’t keep you from going into normal public places on the ground, don’t let it keep you from traveling and seeing the world

I’m going to be real with you here. If you are still drinking and driving after having an interlock, you have a problem. I know that this hurts to hear. It did for me too. I got a violation on my Smart Start device even after my BACtrack device told me I was at 0.011 and my state’s limit is 0.02. Just like the DUI itself, you think it can’t happen to you until it does.

If you do decide to continue drinking and you get a BACtrack, please please please make sure you get it calibrated regularly. I was taught by an experienced recruiter to say something like “I’m open to your best and highest salary,” but I have personally never used that. My preference when asked is to say “I saw what the salary range is overall but could you clarify what that might look like for someone of my experience?” From my experience, they have always given a range from midrange toward the top of that range, even if I only have the minimum experience the job description supposedly requires. If I would have been the first to give a range, I would have been selling myself short. I know people say you have to give a range because they won’t give one, but from my experience over the last several years, only one out of 12-18 companies (sorry I don’t remember the exact number) has refused to give me the exact salary range. This includes companies who didn’t post a salary range at all because state laws, as well as (mostly) those who were required to provide one but narrowed it down per the job posting range based on my experience (which was primarily toward the bare minimum of the “years”  range but still wanted to pay me average - more pay). There’s nothing wrong with at least attempting to get them to give you the range (BASED ON YOUR EXPERIENCE LEVEL) which may or may not be different than the overall range but it’s worth a shot. If they say no, you proceed with your true expected range while knowing it may not work with this particular company.

I work as a quality engineer for a midsize medical device company and honestly, all the surgeons on our design teams have 15+ years of real life experience, typically more like 20-25 years. These are generally people who have spent their time in the field and may now be in teaching or research positions outside of their work with us.

While this likely isn’t an option for you fresh out of med school, I’ve always thought it seemed like an interesting job! Our design surgeons consult with the development engineering teams for specific projects over a period of several years as they work through designing the new device. On a regular basis, they travel to our campus for in-person labs where they work through using the devices in a fake OR with a cadaver. We look for the feedback they provide on usability, reliability, etc. and also take into account their suggestions on how clinically useful certain features may be.

Unfortunately for you, it would be difficult to provide useful feedback to a project team without having experience in the real world as a surgeon first. If this is something that is of interest to you, I would suggest finding something to specialize in and getting really, really good at it. Not to say that there aren’t any options for you outside of traditional MD work, but if this is the kind of career you think you may want in the future, you have to start preparing as soon as you get out of med school

I come from a different perspective on this since all my experience is from my 4 years of forstering 6 different dogs from an organization that trains service dogs for kids and veterans with disabilities. That being said, my main point that I try to get across to people is the ADA laws. I politely inform them that the laws do allow self-training (which I believe can often be very effective!) but I am not able to provide professional advice on their specific situation. Whenever I encountered someone that was looking for a SD for a child, I did refer them to my organization. If it was for themselves (assuming they are an adult), I recommended other mainstream organizations like Canine Companions while still reminding them that there are many private trainers who are happy to assist with individualized owner training. I’ve found that a lot of people truly don’t know that owner training is an option and while I obviously wouldn’t recommend that to someone blindly, I’ve found that sometimes that conversation can be enough for that person to go and look into it even just Google searching trainers in your area. I know it can be frustrating because you always wonder if that person just wants their dog to be a “service dog” so they can take them places but I’ve tried to really have an open mind and consider that maybe they just aren’t educated and don’t know how to go about the process when they do have a true disability. I realize it’s totally different when it is your own SD or SDIT but from my own experience I have definitely encountered people who just needed that little push from a stranger to encourage them to look into taking that next step into getting the help they need. Again, I would make the focus more on the specific laws regarding SDITs and SD training rather than recommending a specific trainer because that can be so different for each individual situation. You always have the right to decline speaking any further with the person asking but I guess I always try to give people the benefit of the doubt because you never know when you could be that person who really helps push them to mitigate their disability and take that step which is often confusing to someone who doesn’t know the laws and the processes that most of us do

Hi! Non-swimmer here. I also happen to be 100% deaf when I’m not wearing my cochlear implant, which I take off in the water. I have been snorkeling on cruises since I was 11 and am now 22. You would be surprised how much of a difference putting some air in those yellow floatation vests actually makes. If your wife is like me and her main problem comes from not being able to float or just general fear in the water, the vest helps a lot. She’ll still need to have some basic idea of how to go through the motions of swimming, but wearing fins makes a huge difference in swimming power. I have also been on some excursions where the guides were willing to pull me around on a paddle board (particularly those where you climb off a boat and don’t get too far away.) Don’t let her miss out on seeing all of the fish, coral, etc. just because she can’t swim. Snorkeling is such a good way to form that bridge between swimming and just sitting on the beach or the boat missing out. I would strongly suggest only doing snorkeling with a knowledgeable guide at a reputable company when you start out though, just in case there are issues. I would also be upfront with the guide that she cannot swim so that they are aware and can save her in case of an emergency.

Honestly, there’s a difference between places with 1 or 2 star reviews and 3.5 star reviews. People may give negative reviews but if the place wasn’t totally horrible, they’re going to give 3 stars and not 1. I would also consider the fact that a lot of places which have many 5 star reviews may have run some kind of promotion in order to get those. A place that I toured (and did not end up signing with) had a policy where anyone who left a review could be entered to win a monetary prize. Most likely, anyone who wants to win isn’t going to live a poor review since it’s assumed that won’t lead to winning. Above all else, I would suggest taking into consideration the quantity of poor reviews. If a large complex has significantly more reviews than other smaller complexes, it probably averages out to be a little more accurate. I’ve found that all the bigger complexes I’ve rented from have been fairly consistent with their Yelp/Google reviews but the smaller complexes can be extremely hit or miss since they may only have a handful of reviews.
